P1-0512.key: Most automation projects happen in plants that are already producing. The hard part is not the new control system. It is changing it around production schedules, legacy equipment and the people who run the line.

P1-0514.key: Why brownfield is harder than greenfield

P1-0515.key: In a new plant, the control system is designed together with everything else. In a running plant it has to fit around what is already there: PLC generations that no longer talk to each other, OEM packages with closed controls, changes made over the years that were never documented, and a production schedule that leaves short windows for change.

P1-0516.key: The risk sits in the gaps: an interlock nobody wrote down, a network dependency that appears on start-up day, or an operator workaround that was quietly holding the process together.

P1-0518.key: Separate control islands make batches harder to repeat and records harder to keep. Manual batching and fixed-speed equipment limit capacity, consistency and traceability. Reports are compiled by hand, spares for obsolete hardware get harder to find, and more of the plant’s know-how ends up in a few people’s heads.

P1-0521.key: I/O lists, drawings, PLC and HMI versions, networks, panels, and how operators actually run the process. Mark what works, what is at end of life and what is undocumented.

P1-0523.key: Reactors, vessels and drives in good condition can usually stay. Automate and connect them, and replace only where the risk or the gain justifies it.

P1-0525.key: For batch plants, an ISA-88 structure separates equipment from recipes, so products and procedures can change without rewriting code, and every batch leaves a record.

P1-0527.key: Test the new logic against the agreed specification at factory acceptance, then confirm it on site. A URS, FDS, FAT and SAT give every stakeholder the same reference.

P1-0529.key: Stage the change area by area around shutdowns, with fall-back plans, trained operators and support on site through start-up.

P1-0533.key: Research laboratory. Existing metal-extraction reactors retained and automated with pH control, dosing, temperature, agitation and PLC / SCADA, ready for future scale.

P1-0536.key: Cleaning-product manufacturer, Canada. Automated compounding with 26 VFDs and 4 agitators, ISA-88 recipes and a paperless audit trail, with 15% energy and material saved.

P1-0537.key: I/O linked to an existing DCS

P1-0538.key: Global healthcare company, Toronto. Adjuvant and CIP skid automation to 21 CFR Part 11, with ISA-88 sequencing and OPC UA links to the plant’s existing DCS, documented from URS to SAT.

P1-0540.key: Dairy, California. A centralized control system across all areas, with more than 2,000 I/O and {PlantON} for CIP validation and traceability.

P1-0542.key: Retrofitting is not always the answer. Replace when hardware is past support and spares have become a production risk, when the process has changed enough that the old control philosophy no longer fits, or when safety or compliance requirements cannot be met on the existing platform. The audit in step one is what lets you make that call on evidence rather than habit.

P1-0543.key: Audit what you have before you decide what to replace.

P1-0544.key: Keep equipment that still works; automate and connect it.

P1-0545.key: Structure batch control so recipes and records are repeatable.

P1-0546.key: Test before site, and cut over in planned windows.

P1-0552.key: Planning a modernization in a running plant?

P1-0553.key: How to modernize controls in a plant that is already producing: audit first, keep what works, test before site and cut over in planned windows.

P1-0554.key: Modernize a Running Plant | Instron Technologies

P1-0555.key: Modernize a running plant without starting again, Instron Technologies

P1-0557.key: Start with one loss. Plant data people actually use.

P1-0558.key: Most plant-data projects do not fail on technology. They stall between a promising pilot and the second line. This is the rollout sequence we use with process plants to keep that from happening.

P1-0560.key: Most plants already collect plenty of data. PLCs, SCADA, utility meters, recipe systems and quality records each hold part of the picture. What is usually missing is operating context: which batch, which line, which shift and which loss a number belongs to.

P1-0561.key: In our experience, projects stall for four reasons:

P1-0562.key: The goal is “visibility” rather than a specific loss, so nobody can say whether the pilot worked.

P1-0563.key: Dashboards are built for managers, and the people who run the line never use them.

P1-0564.key: Machines and areas from different suppliers report in different ways, so their figures cannot be compared.

P1-0565.key: The plan tries to connect everything at once, and runs out of budget or patience halfway through.

P1-0567.key: The cost shows up in hours and in waste. At a California dairy we worked with, pasteurizer trends and utility figures were compiled by hand across more than 12 separate control systems. Compliance reporting took up to two hours a day, and there was little link between utility use and production.

P1-0568.key: That pattern is common. When data has no context, people rebuild it in spreadsheets, and the effort goes into reporting instead of improving.

P1-0571.key: Downtime on a critical cell, chemical use per batch, utility use per unit of output, or hours spent on reports. If you cannot put a number on it today, measuring it is the first win.

P1-0572.key: Prove it on one line or area

P1-0573.key: Connect only what that loss needs. Record a baseline first, so the result is a before-and-after in your own figures rather than a vendor estimate.

P1-0575.key: The people on the line define the downtime reasons, check the numbers and choose the screens they will use. Their trust decides whether the system outlives the pilot.

P1-0577.key: Turn the pilot result into a short business case: what changed, what it is worth per year and what it took. That is what funds the next phase.

P1-0578.key: Agree one model before you scale

P1-0579.key: Machines and areas never designed to report the same way need a common performance model, rolled up by machine, line and shift. Decide it once, not line by line.

P1-0581.key: Add areas in order of value. Keep legacy equipment that still works and connect it, rather than replacing it just to make the data easier.

P1-0582.key: What it looks like in practice

P1-0584.key: Dairy, California. More than 12 control systems on one platform, with traceability from raw-milk reception to dispatch. Reporting went from up to two hours to about seven minutes, with 12% less chemical and 11% less utility use.

P1-0586.key: Die casting. Legacy machines and ERP data connected into one plant performance view without replacing equipment, with 37% fewer rejects.

P1-0588.key: Manufacturing. A common performance model for machines never designed to report the same way, rolled up by machine, line and shift.

P1-0590.key: The software matters less than how it is connected to your process. Before you choose a partner, ask:

P1-0591.key: Can they work with what you have?

P1-0592.key: Most plants run a mix of PLC generations and OEM packages. A partner should be comfortable connecting them, not only replacing them.

P1-0594.key: Batch phases, CIP, utilities and quality limits decide what a number means. Process and automation knowledge matter as much as the dashboard.

P1-0595.key: Who owns the model when they leave?

P1-0596.key: Tags, downtime reasons and reports should be documented and handed over, so your team can extend them without starting again.

P1-0597.key: {PlantON} is our plant-data platform for batch and continuous process plants. We deliver it together with the automation and process work around it, so the data has context from the first day.

P1-0598.key: Pick one loss that costs money, and measure it before you connect anything else.

P1-0599.key: Prove the gain on one line or area, in the plant’s own numbers.

P1-0600.key: Agree one performance model before you scale, so every machine and area reports the same way.

P1-0601.key: Expand in phases, and connect legacy equipment that still works instead of replacing it.
